questions.question: A 35-year-old patient who was mistakenly prescribed topical corticosteroid eye drops for a dendritic corneal ulcer presents 1 week later with marked worsening of vision, photophobia, and a large, wide, amoebic corneal ulcer with scalloped geographic margins staining with fluorescein. Which of the following statements is correct regarding this presentation?

options.A: The large geographic ulceration is due to topical corticosteroid misuse
options.B: Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) is the primary causative pathogen
options.C: This condition presents exclusively during primary childhood infection
options.D: First-line therapy consists exclusively of systemic acyclovir monotherapy

questions.explanation:
Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) keratitis typically presents with classic linear branching epithelial dendritic ulcers with terminal end-bulbs. If topical corticosteroids are erroneously prescribed in active herpetic epithelial keratitis, local cell-mediated immunity is profoundly suppressed while viral replication explodes unchecked. The delicate dendrites coalesce and expand outwards, transforming into a massive, wide, amoebic-shaped 'geographic ulcer' with scalloped, devitalized margins. Topical steroids are strictly contraindicated in active epithelial herpetic disease.

HIGH-YIELD: Herpetic Keratitis Rules of Thumb:
• True Dendritic Ulcer: Linear branching ulcer with terminal bulbs + reduced corneal sensation (anesthesia).
• Steroid Disaster: Topical steroids + HSV dendrite = Geographic (Amoebic) Ulcer.
• Treatment: Topical Ganciclovir 0.15% gel (5 times daily) OR Oral Acyclovir 400 mg (5 times daily).

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: NEVER prescribe topical corticosteroids for an undiagnosed red eye or active dendritic corneal ulcer! Steroids fuel herpetic replication, leading to corneal melt and perforation.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A large geographic ulcer that develops after topical corticosteroid use in herpetic dendritic keratitis is due to steroid misuse; the causative virus is HSV-1.
optionExplanations.B: HSV-1 is responsible for >95% of ocular herpes infections in adults; HSV-2 is rare and associated with neonatal transmission.
optionExplanations.C: Epithelial dendritic/geographic keratitis is a manifestation of secondary viral reactivation from latency in the trigeminal ganglion, not primary infection (which is usually a mild follicular conjunctivitis).
optionExplanations.D: Management centers on immediate cessation of steroids and initiation of topical antiviral therapy (Ganciclovir 0.15% gel or Trifluridine 1% drops) or oral acyclovir/valacyclovir.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that topical corticosteroid misuse converts herpetic dendritic ulcers into large, vision-threatening geographic ulcers.

questions.question: A corneal surgeon is evaluating donor corneal tissue from an eye bank prior to performing penetrating keratoplasty for a recipient with pseudophakic bullous keratopathy. Which of the following statements is correct regarding donor tissue viability?

options.A: Corneal graft clarity and long-term functional survival are directly dependent on the donor endothelial cell density
options.B: The donor corneal endothelium actively regenerates by mitosis postoperatively
options.C: Donor tissue can be safely utilized regardless of endothelial cell count as long as Bowman's layer is intact
options.D: Epithelial cell survival is the sole determinant of graft rejection

questions.explanation:
The corneal endothelium is a non-regenerative monolayer of hexagonal cells that lines the posterior surface of the cornea. Endothelial cells possess active Na+/K+-ATPase metabolic pumps that constantly dehydrate the hydrophilic corneal stroma, maintaining deturgescence and optical clarity. Human endothelial cells are arrested in the G1 phase of the cell cycle and do NOT divide in vivo; cell loss is compensated solely by cell enlargement (polymegathism) and shape change (pleomorphism). Therefore, pre-transplant donor tissue viability and long-term graft survival are strictly dependent on adequate endothelial cell density (typically >2,000 to 2,500 cells/mm² on specular microscopy).

HIGH-YIELD: Corneal Endothelium Facts:
• Normal adult count: ~2,500–3,000 cells/mm².
• Critical threshold for corneal decompensation/edema: <500–700 cells/mm².
• Eye bank donor release criterion: Minimum >2,000–2,200 cells/mm².

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Corneal endothelium does not divide: When endothelial cells die from trauma, surgery, or aging, the remaining cells simply stretch out; once count drops below 500 cells/mm², irreversible bullous keratopathy occurs.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The corneal endothelium does not regenerate, so graft clarity and long-term survival depend on donor endothelial cell density.
optionExplanations.B: Human corneal endothelial cells do NOT regenerate or undergo mitosis in vivo.
optionExplanations.C: Endothelial cell count is the paramount metric; Bowman's layer integrity has no pump function.
optionExplanations.D: Endothelial rejection (characterized by the Khodadoust line) is the most catastrophic form of graft rejection, not epithelial.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that corneal graft clarity and surgical success depend directly on donor endothelial cell density because endothelial cells do not regenerate.

questions.question: A 60-year-old patient with long-standing chronic anterior uveitis and secondary glaucoma presents with foreign body sensation and visual decline. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy reveals a horizontal, chalky white-gray band extending across the interpalpebral cornea, featuring small clear round holes ('Swiss-cheese appearance') separated from the limbus by a clear lucid interval. What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism of this condition?

options.A: Extracellular deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite in Bowman's layer and anterior stroma
options.B: Intracellular copper accumulation in Descemet's membrane
options.D: Cholesterol and phospholipid infiltration into peripheral stroma

questions.explanation:
Band keratopathy is a corneal degeneration characterized by the extracellular deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite salts within the epithelial basement membrane, Bowman's layer, and superficial anterior stroma. It classically presents in the interpalpebral fissure (where tear evaporation increases local calcium and phosphate concentration and elevates tear pH). The clear holes within the band represent areas where corneal nerve fibers penetrate Bowman's layer ('Swiss-cheese pattern'). Etiologies include chronic ocular inflammation (chronic anterior uveitis in JIA), chronic hypercalcemia (hyperparathyroidism, renal failure, sarcoidosis, vitamin D toxicity), and long-standing phthisis bulbi. Treatment involves topical chelation using disodium EDTA.

HIGH-YIELD: Band Keratopathy Essentials:
• Pathology: Calcium phosphate / hydroxyapatite in Bowman's membrane.
• Appearance: Horizontal interpalpebral white band with Swiss-cheese holes, separated from limbus by a clear zone.
• Causes: JIA-associated chronic uveitis (most common ocular cause!), Hyperparathyroidism, End-stage renal disease.
• Definitive Treatment: Superficial debridement followed by 1.5–3.0% Disodium EDTA chelation.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Notice the clear zone between the calcified band and the limbus: The limbal arcade has rich buffering capacity that prevents local tissue alkalization and calcium precipitation!

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Band keratopathy is calcium (hydroxyapatite) deposition in the epithelial basement membrane, Bowman's layer and anterior stroma, with a clear lucid interval at the limbus.
optionExplanations.B: Copper accumulation in Descemet's membrane forms a Kayser-Fleischer ring in Wilson disease.
optionExplanations.C: Amyloid deposition occurs in lattice corneal dystrophy.
optionExplanations.D: Lipid/cholesterol infiltration forms arcus senilis in the peripheral cornea.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify band keratopathy as calcium hydroxyapatite deposition in Bowman's layer, classically associated with chronic uveitis and systemic hypercalcemia.

questions.question: A patient with a history of recurrent herpes simplex keratitis is examined using a fine wisp of sterile cotton touched lightly to the central cornea of the right eye. The patient fails to exhibit a bilateral blink reflex and reports no sensation. Which of the following correctly describes the anatomical and physiological basis of this test result?

options.A: The patient does not blink due to desensitization and loss of afferent input via the nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1)
options.B: The patient directly closes his eyes due to normal trigeminal function
options.C: The primary treatment for this condition is topical prophylactic antibiotic monotherapy
options.D: The patient fails to blink due to denervation of the infraorbital sensory nerve
options.E: It is strongly advised to treat this condition with intensive topical corticosteroids

questions.explanation:
The corneal reflex assesses the afferent and efferent integrity of the sensory and motor reflex arc: (1) Afferent arm: mediated by sensory fibers traveling from the cornea through the long and short ciliary nerves to the nasociliary nerve, a branch of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1), synapsing in the spinal trigeminal nucleus. (2) Efferent arm: interneurons project bilaterally to the facial motor nuclei (CN VII), innervating both orbicularis oculi muscles to produce a bilateral blink. In neurotrophic keratitis (caused by HSV, HZO, acoustic neuroma, or stroke), damage to the nasociliary branch abolishes the afferent limb, resulting in corneal anesthesia and absent bilateral blinking.

HIGH-YIELD: Corneal Reflex Anatomy:
• Afferent limb: CN V1 (Ophthalmic -> Nasociliary nerve).
• Efferent limb: CN VII (Facial nerve -> Orbicularis oculi bilateral blink).
• Touching one cornea produces a DIRECT and a CONSENSUAL blink.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: A lesion of CN V1 causes ABSENT blinks in BOTH eyes when touching the affected cornea, but NORMAL bilateral blinks when touching the contralateral sound cornea. In contrast, a CN VII lesion blinks only on the intact facial side regardless of which eye is touched.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The afferent limb of the corneal reflex runs through the nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1); loss of the blink indicates corneal anesthesia, as can follow herpetic keratitis.
optionExplanations.B: Normal response is an instantaneous, bilateral, symmetric blink.
optionExplanations.C: Topical antibiotics do not restore nerve function; neurotrophic keratitis requires aggressive lubrication, nerve growth factor (cenegermin), or tarsorrhaphy.
optionExplanations.D: The infraorbital nerve is a branch of V2 supplying the cheek and lower lid, having no sensory distribution to the cornea.
optionExplanations.E: Corticosteroids are strictly contraindicated in neurotrophic epithelial breakdown due to massive risk of stromal melting and perforation.

questions.educationalObjective: Understand that the afferent limb of the corneal blink reflex is mediated by the nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1).

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with a severe, painful red eye. Which of the following clinical features most reliably differentiates anterior scleritis from episcleritis?

options.A: Blanchable vascular redness that completely disappears following topical phenylephrine application
options.B: Scleritis is a mild, self-limiting condition compared to episcleritis
options.C: Severe, deep, boring ocular pain that radiates to the brow and temple and awakens the patient at night
options.D: Scleritis is strictly an isolated idiopathic disorder that is never associated with systemic connective tissue diseases

questions.explanation:
The cardinal distinguishing symptom of scleritis is severe, deep, boring, agonizing ocular pain. This pain characteristically radiates along the branches of CN V1 to the forehead, brow, cheek, and temple, is exacerbated by eye movements, and characteristically awakens the patient from sleep. In stark contrast, episcleritis causes only mild discomfort, foreign body grittiness, or localized tenderness without severe pain. Furthermore, scleritis features deep violaceous/bluish scleral edema that does NOT blanch with phenylephrine and is strongly associated (>50% of cases) with systemic autoimmune diseases (most notably rheumatoid arthritis and granulomatosis with polyangiitis).

HIGH-YIELD: Clinical Comparison:
• Episcleritis: Mild discomfort, bright red, movable vessels, BLANCHES with phenylephrine, rarely systemic.
• Scleritis: SEVERE BORING PAIN (wakes patient at night), violaceous bluish-red, deep fixed vessels, DOES NOT BLANCH, >50% autoimmune (RA, GPA, SLE).

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Scleritis in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis is a marker of severe, active systemic rheumatoid vasculitis associated with significantly increased systemic mortality!

optionExplanations.A: Blanching with phenylephrine is the hallmark of benign episcleritis, not scleritis.
optionExplanations.B: Scleritis is a potentially blinding, necrotizing emergency that can lead to scleral thinning, staphyloma, and globe perforation.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Severe, deep, boring pain that radiates to the brow and temple and wakes the patient at night is the hallmark of scleritis; episcleritis is mild and its redness blanches with phenylephrine.
optionExplanations.D: More than 50% of patients with scleritis have an underlying systemic autoimmune connective tissue disease.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize severe boring pain radiating to the brow and waking the patient at night as the hallmark differentiator of scleritis from episcleritis.

questions.question: A patient is evaluated 18 months following an uncomplicated penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) for keratoconus. The donor graft is thin, clear, and perfectly epithelialized. However, the patient is unable to achieve acceptable vision with standard spectacles. What is the most common late optical complication encountered following this procedure?
questions.explanation:
High irregular refractive astigmatism is well-established as the most common late complication and primary optical cause of poor uncorrected visual acuity following penetrating keratoplasty (PKP). Because full-thickness transplantation involves cutting a 360-degree circular donor and host interface and securing it with 16–24 sutures, subtle microscopic variations in trephination circularity, suture depth, uneven radial tension, and asymmetric host cicatrization lead to significant corneal toricity and irregular astigmatism (frequently >4.0 to 6.0 D).

HIGH-YIELD: Managing Post-PKP Astigmatism:
• Topography-guided selective suture removal (cut sutures along the steep meridian).
• Rigid Gas Permeable (RGP) or Scleral contact lenses (neutralizes irregular anterior corneal tear lens).
• Astigmatic keratotomy or femtosecond relaxing incisions.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Do not remove all graft sutures prematurely: Sutures must remain in place for at least 12–18 months in PKP because corneal stroma heals extremely slowly without vascularization.

optionExplanations.A: Infectious ulcers can occur around loose sutures, but are less common than refractive error in intact grafts.
optionExplanations.B: Cataract formation can be accelerated by postoperative steroid regimens, but refractive astigmatism is the primary universal challenge.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. High irregular astigmatism is the most common late optical complication after penetrating keratoplasty, limiting vision despite a clear graft.
optionExplanations.D: Retinal detachment is a recognized vitreoretinal complication, occurring in <2%–3% of anterior segment grafts.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify high irregular astigmatism as the most frequent late optical complication limiting uncorrected visual acuity after penetrating keratoplasty.

questions.question: A 22-year-old university student presents to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of severe ocular pain, photophobia, decreased vision, and purulent discharge from her right eye. She admits to sleeping in her soft contact lenses and rinsing her lens case with tap water. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy reveals a dense, rapidly progressing, yellowish-green suppurative stromal infiltrate with a 4 mm epithelial defect and a 1.5 mm hypopyon in the anterior chamber. What is the most likely causative pathogen?
questions.explanation:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a virulent gram-negative aerobic bacillus and the single most common and dangerous causative pathogen in contact lens-related bacterial keratitis (accounting for >60% of cases). Pseudomonas produces potent proteases, elastases, and exotoxins (Exotoxin A) that cause rapid, fulminant liquefactive necrosis of the corneal stroma. The hallmark presentation is a rapidly spreading stromal infiltrate with copious, adherent, yellowish-green purulent discharge and early hypopyon formation. Left untreated, Pseudomonas can cause full-thickness corneal perforation within 24 to 48 hours. Management requires immediate corneal scrapings for Gram stain and culture, followed by emergent intensive hourly empiric fortified topical broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., fortified Tobramycin + Cefazolin/Vancomycin) or high-dose fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin).

HIGH-YIELD: Pseudomonas Keratitis Key Points:
• Patient Profile: Extended-wear soft contact lens wearer.
• Clinical Hallmarks: Yellow-green purulent discharge + rapidly spreading liquefactive necrosis + Hypopyon.
• Emergency: Can perforate cornea in 24–48 hours!
• Treatment: Emergent empiric hourly fortified topical antibiotics (Tobramycin + Cefazolin) or 4th-generation fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin). NEVER PATCH!

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Never prescribe topical steroids or patch the eye in suspected contact lens keratitis; steroids will accelerate Pseudomonas collagenolysis and cause corneal perforation.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A rapidly progressing yellow-green suppurative corneal infiltrate with hypopyon in a soft contact lens wearer is classically caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
optionExplanations.B: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of non-contact lens bacterial keratitis, presenting with a round, localized, well-demarcated creamy-white infiltrate.
optionExplanations.C: Streptococcus pneumoniae produces deep suppurative ulceration with a progressive undermining edge, often post-trauma.
optionExplanations.D: Candida albicans keratitis presents indolently in pre-existing compromised or immunosuppressed eyes with a suppurative 'collar-button' infiltrate.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify Pseudomonas aeruginosa as the most frequent and destructive pathogen responsible for contact lens-associated bacterial keratitis.

questions.question: An emergency physician applies a paper strip impregnated with sodium fluorescein to the lower bulbar conjunctiva to evaluate a patient with suspected corneal injury. Which of the following statements regarding this diagnostic test is TRUE?

options.A: Fluorescein dye spontaneously emits high-intensity blue light
options.B: Fluorescein is activated and viewed under monochromatic yellow illumination
options.C: It is used clinically to assess the structural integrity of the corneal epithelium
options.D: The test utilizes standard unfiltered white halogen light for fluorescence visualization
options.E: The excitation filter required for fluorescence is green light

questions.explanation:
Sodium fluorescein is a water-soluble dye widely used to assess the integrity of the corneal epithelium. Intact healthy corneal epithelium possesses tight junctions (zonula occludens) and a hydrophobic lipid surface that repels fluorescein. However, when corneal epithelial cells are absent, damaged, or desquamated (e.g., corneal abrasion, ulcer, punctate keratitis, or Seidel's wound leak), the hydrophilic fluorescein dye enters the extracellular spaces of the exposed corneal stroma and fluoresces bright green when excited by cobalt blue light (~490 nm wavelength).

HIGH-YIELD: Fluorescein Diagnostic Utility:
• Corneal Abrasion: Stains epithelial defects bright green under cobalt blue filter.
• Seidel Test: Dilution of concentrated orange fluorescein by escaping aqueous humor demonstrates full-thickness corneal perforation / wound leak (bright green streaming rivulet under blue light).
• Tear Break-Up Time (TBUT): Evaluates tear film stability (<10 seconds indicates tear film instability/dry eye).

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Remember that fluorescein stains exposed STROMA and intercellular spaces where epithelium is missing; it does NOT stain devitalized virus-infected cells (which are stained by Rose Bengal or Lissamine Green).

optionExplanations.A: Fluorescein is a fluorescent dye; it absorbs light at one wavelength (blue) and emits light at a longer wavelength (green), it does not emit blue light.
optionExplanations.B: Option B & E: The excitation light source is cobalt blue light (~490 nm), not yellow or green.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Fluorescein stains areas where the corneal epithelium is disrupted, so it is used to assess epithelial integrity.
optionExplanations.D: Under white light, fluorescein appears faint orange/yellow; fluorescence is only visualized using a cobalt blue filter.
optionExplanations.E: Option B & E: The excitation light source is cobalt blue light (~490 nm), not yellow or green.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that sodium fluorescein dye under cobalt blue illumination is used to evaluate corneal epithelial integrity.

questions.question: A 45-year-old agricultural worker who spends long hours outdoors in sunny climates presents with a triangular fleshy growth extending across his nasal bulbar conjunctiva onto the nasal cornea. Which definition best describes the fundamental histopathological finding of this lesion?

options.A: Chronic acute inflammation and suppuration of the eyelid margin
options.B: Elastotic degeneration of subconjunctival connective tissue leading to a fibrovascular membrane that invades the cornea
options.C: Malignant squamous intraepithelial neoplasia of the limbus
options.D: Granulomatous lipogranuloma of the meibomian glands

questions.explanation:
A pterygium is a benign, wing-shaped, triangular fibrovascular growth of degenerated subconjunctival tissue that proliferates and invades across the limbus onto the superficial cornea, dissolving Bowman's layer. Its underlying pathophysiology is elastotic degeneration (actinic elastosis) of collagen within the subepithelial connective tissue, triggered by chronic, lifelong exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation, heat, dry wind, and dust. Histologically, abnormal basophilic, elastotic degenerated collagen fibers proliferate with prominent vascularization.

HIGH-YIELD: Pterygium Essentials:
• Major Risk Factor: Chronic Ultraviolet (UV-B) light exposure ('surfer's / farmer's eye').
• Pathology: Elastotic degeneration of subconjunctival collagen.
• Clinical Anatomy: Located on nasal bulbar conjunctiva; crosses limbus onto cornea.
• Visual threat: Induces with-the-rule corneal astigmatism and can directly occlude the central pupillary visual axis.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Differentiate pterygium (CROSSES the limbus onto the cornea) from pinguecula (CONFINED to conjunctiva, NEVER crosses the limbus!).

optionExplanations.A: Describes blepharitis, not pterygium.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Pterygium shows elastotic degeneration of subconjunctival tissue that forms a fibrovascular membrane growing onto the cornea, related to chronic UV exposure.
optionExplanations.C: Ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN) is a dysplastic/malignant lesion featuring gelatinous or leukoplakic epithelial atypia.
optionExplanations.D: Describes a chalazion of the eyelid.

questions.educationalObjective: Define pterygium as an elastotic degeneration of subconjunctival connective tissue forming a fibrovascular growth that invades the cornea.

questions.question: A 38-year-old schoolteacher presents with acute-onset redness, watery discharge, and gritty foreign body sensation in his right eye, which spread to his left eye 3 days later. His 7-year-old son had identical symptoms 2 weeks ago. On examination, there is marked follicular conjunctival reaction, chemosis, petechial subconjunctival hemorrhages, and a tender, palpable preauricular lymph node on the right. Which of the following statements is correct regarding this condition?

options.A: Initiate immediate topical antiviral drops (e.g., trifluridine)
options.B: Tender, painful periocular (preauricular) lymphadenopathy is a hallmark clinical feature
options.C: The disease is caused by bacterial colonization of the Meibomian glands
options.D: Topical aminoglycoside drops are curative and shorten disease transmission

questions.explanation:
Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) is a highly contagious, severe form of viral conjunctivitis caused by Adenovirus (serotypes 8, 19, and 37). It spreads rapidly via direct hand-to-eye contact, contaminated finger-to-surface fomites, and shared towels. The hallmark diagnostic tetrad consists of: (1) acute bilateral (often sequential) watery conjunctivitis with prominent inferior palpebral conjunctival follicles, (2) painful/tender preauricular lymphadenopathy (palpable anterior to the tragus), (3) pseudomembranes on the palpebral conjunctiva in severe cases, and (4) subepithelial corneal infiltrates developing 1–2 weeks after onset (immune complex deposition). Management is supportive with cool compresses and artificial tears; strict hand hygiene is critical to prevent institutional transmission.

HIGH-YIELD: Adenoviral Conjunctivitis Hallmarks:
• Presentation: Profuse watery discharge + Follicular conjunctival reaction + TENDER PREAURICULAR LYMPHADENOPATHY.
• Transmission: Extreme contagion (adenovirus resists desiccation; contagiousness persists for 10–14 days!).
• Management: Strict handwashing, quarantine from school/work, cold compresses, preservative-free tears.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Do not confuse adenoviral conjunctivitis with bacterial conjunctivitis: Bacterial features thick purulent morning eyelid crusting with NO preauricular adenopathy (except in hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis).

optionExplanations.A: Topical antivirals (acyclovir/ganciclovir) are completely ineffective against adenoviruses and cause toxic keratopathy.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Tender, palpable preauricular lymphadenopathy is a hallmark of adenoviral epidemic keratoconjunctivitis.
optionExplanations.C: Option C & D: The condition is viral; topical antibiotics offer zero therapeutic benefit and do not prevent spread.
optionExplanations.D: Option C & D: The condition is viral; topical antibiotics offer zero therapeutic benefit and do not prevent spread. Topical aminoglycosides cause contact allergy and epithelial toxicity.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify tender preauricular lymphadenopathy and watery follicular conjunctivitis as the classic hallmarks of adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis.

questions.question: A 52-year-old construction worker presents with a fleshy fibrovascular triangular lesion originating from the nasal bulbar conjunctiva that has crossed the limbus and encroached 3.5 mm across the cornea, causing 2.5 diopters of induced astigmatism. Which of the following statements is true regarding definitive management?

options.A: It is a pterygium, and definitive management is surgical excision (with conjunctival autograft)
options.B: It is a pterygium, and definitive treatment is Argon laser photocoagulation
options.C: It is a pinguecula, and must be treated with immediate cryotherapy
options.D: Medical therapy with topical antihistamines will cause complete lesion regression

questions.explanation:
When a pterygium becomes visually significant (induces corneal astigmatism, directly threatens the central optical zone/ pupil, causes chronic foreign body sensation, or restricts ocular motility), surgical excision is the definitive management. To prevent the historically high recurrence rate (which exceeds 50% with simple 'bare sclera' excision), modern surgical excision is combined with a limbal-conjunctival autograft (harvested from the superior bulbar conjunctiva) secured with fibrin glue or fine sutures, which reduces recurrence rates to <5%. Laser photocoagulation has no role in pterygium treatment.

HIGH-YIELD: Surgical Indications for Pterygium: 1. Encroachment onto visual axis threatening central vision 2. Progressive induced irregular astigmatism 3. Restriction of ocular motility (diplopia) 4. Unacceptable chronic redness, irritation, or cosmesis.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Bare sclera excision alone is obsolete due to a 50–80% recurrence rate; conjunctival autografting or amniotic membrane grafting is the standard of care.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A fibrovascular lesion crossing the limbus onto the cornea is a pterygium; when visually significant (induced astigmatism), surgical excision with conjunctival autograft is the definitive treatment.
optionExplanations.B: Lasers cannot excise fibrovascular pterygium tissue and can induce scleral necrosis.
optionExplanations.C: A pinguecula does not cross the limbus and does not require cryotherapy.
optionExplanations.D: Eye drops (lubricants, mild topical steroids) only provide temporary symptomatic relief for acute pterygitis, but cannot reverse the fibrovascular growth.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that visually significant pterygium is managed definitively with surgical excision combined with a conjunctival autograft.

questions.question: A 6-week-old neonate presents with persistent unilateral conjunctival hyperemia and mucopurulent ocular discharge. The mother received limited prenatal care. Based on clinical guidelines for neonatal conjunctival infections (ophthalmia neonatorum), what is the mandatory immediate next step?

options.A: Obtaining conjunctival swabs and scrapings for Gram stain, Giemsa stain, and bacterial/ chlamydial culture or PCR is mandatory
options.B: Prescribe topical corticosteroid drops and discharge with reassurance
options.D: Patch the affected eye and re-evaluate at 6 months

questions.explanation:
Ophthalmia neonatorum (neonatal conjunctivitis) occurring within the first 4–6 weeks of life requires urgent microbiological identification because infectious etiologies can be sight-threatening or life-threatening. The major infectious pathogens are: (1) Neisseria gonorrhoeae (presents at days 2–5 with hyperacute, copious, purulent discharge; can rapidly penetrate intact cornea causing corneal perforation and blindness; requires immediate IV/IM ceftriaxone), and (2) Chlamydia trachomatis (the most common infectious cause in the USA, presenting at days 5–14 with mucopurulent discharge and pseudomembranes; associated with chlamydial interstitial pneumonitis; requires oral erythromycin). Immediate conjunctival swab/scraping for Gram stain, culture, and PCR is mandatory to guide targeted systemic therapy.

HIGH-YIELD: Ophthalmia Neonatorum Chronology:
• <24 hours: Chemical conjunctivitis (silver nitrate prophylaxis, mild, self-limiting).
• 2–5 days: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (hyperacute, copious pus, risk of corneal melt -> IV Ceftriaxone!).
• 5–14 days: Chlamydia trachomatis (most common cause -> Oral Erythromycin to treat ocular disease and prevent chlamydial pneumonia!).
• 1–2 weeks: HSV (vesicles, dendritic keratitis -> IV Acyclovir).

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Chlamydia conjunctivitis in a neonate CANNOT be treated with topical antibiotics alone; systemic oral erythromycin is mandatory to eradicate nasopharyngeal colonization and prevent life-threatening chlamydial pneumonia!

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Neonatal conjunctivitis requires conjunctival swabs/scrapings for Gram and Giemsa stains and culture or PCR to identify the organism, including chlamydia.
optionExplanations.B: Topical steroids are strictly contraindicated in active infectious conjunctivitis.
optionExplanations.C: Lensectomy is an intraocular lens surgery, completely unrelated to conjunctivitis.
optionExplanations.D: Eye patching is contraindicated in purulent infections because it traps bacterial toxins against the cornea.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that conjunctival swabbing for Gram stain, culture, and PCR is mandatory in suspected ophthalmia neonatorum.

questions.question: A 48-year-old gardener presents with an asymptomatic, slightly elevated, yellowish-white, triangular nodule on the nasal bulbar conjunctiva adjacent to the limbus. Slit-lamp examination confirms that the lesion does not invade or cross the limbus onto the cornea. Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding this condition?

options.A: Pterygium usually requires no treatment and never affects vision
options.B: A pinguecula is a fibrovascular growth that extends onto the cornea
options.C: A pterygium does not invade the cornea and remains strictly confined to the conjunctiva
options.D: A pinguecula usually requires no active treatment other than reassurance and lubrication
options.E: A pinguecula commonly causes marked irregular corneal astigmatism similar to advanced pterygium

questions.explanation:
A pinguecula is a benign, extremely common degeneration of the bulbar conjunctiva characterized by elastotic degeneration and hyaline deposition in the subconjunctival stroma. It presents as an elevated, yellowish, fatty-appearing patch on the interpalpebral bulbar conjunctiva (most commonly nasal), immediately adjacent to the limbus. Crucially, a pinguecula NEVER crosses the limbus onto the cornea (unlike a pterygium). It is entirely benign, does not induce astigmatism, and usually requires no treatment beyond patient reassurance, UV-protective sunglasses, and ocular lubricants. If acute inflammation occurs (pingueculitis), a brief course of topical NSAIDs or mild steroids may be used.

HIGH-YIELD: Pinguecula vs. Pterygium Comparison:
• Pinguecula: Yellowish elevated nodule, CONFINED to bulbar conjunctiva, does NOT cross limbus, no astigmatism, reassurance/lubrication.
• Pterygium: Triangular fibrovascular wing, CROSSES limbus onto cornea, causes astigmatism, requires surgical autograft excision if visually threatening.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Remember the limbal boundary: If it stops at the limbus = Pinguecula. If it crosses the limbus onto the cornea = Pterygium.

optionExplanations.A: Option A is false: Pterygium frequently induces astigmatism and can invade the central optical axis, causing severe visual loss.
optionExplanations.B: Option B & C are false: By definition, pinguecula is confined to the conjunctiva and NEVER invades the cornea, whereas pterygium directly invades the cornea.
optionExplanations.C: Option B & C are false: By definition, pinguecula is confined to the conjunctiva and NEVER invades the cornea, whereas pterygium directly invades the cornea.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A pinguecula stays on the conjunctiva, does not cross the limbus, and usually needs only reassurance and lubrication.
optionExplanations.E: Option E is false: Pingueculae do not alter corneal curvature and do not induce astigmatism.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify pinguecula as a benign conjunctival elastotic degeneration that does not invade the cornea and typically requires no treatment.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents with deep throbbing pain, photophobia, and blurred vision in his right eye. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy reveals inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber, ciliary flush, and an irregular, misshapen ('festooned') pupil with focal fibrous adhesions tethering the pupillary margin of the iris to the anterior lens capsule. What is the predominant clinical sign?
questions.explanation:
Posterior synechiae are inflammatory adhesions formed between the posterior pigmented iris epithelial margin and the anterior capsule of the crystalline lens. They are a classic hallmark complication of acute and recurrent anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis). Inflammatory exudate rich in fibrin allows the inflamed iris to stick to the lens, causing the pupil to assume an irregular, cloverleaf or 'festooned' shape, especially when dilated with mydriatics. If synechiae extend 360 degrees (seclusio pupillae), aqueous humor cannot pass from the posterior to the anterior chamber, resulting in iris bombé and secondary acute angle-closure glaucoma.

HIGH-YIELD: Posterior Synechiae Clinical Pearls:
• Pathology: Adhesions between iris and anterior lens capsule.
• Treatment: Strong cycloplegic/mydriatic drops (Atropine 1%, Cyclopentolate 1%, Phenylephrine 10%) to break existing adhesions and prevent new ones by keeping the pupil mobile and dilated.
• Major Complication: Seclusio pupillae (360-degree adhesion) -> Iris bombé -> Secondary angle-closure glaucoma.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Do not confuse posterior synechiae (iris adhering to lens) with anterior synechiae (iris adhering to peripheral cornea/ trabecular meshwork in the anterior chamber angle).

optionExplanations.A: Aqueous flare is the optical scattering of slit-lamp light (Tyndall effect) caused by elevated protein in the anterior chamber.
optionExplanations.B: Mature cataract causes diffuse white opacification of the entire lens.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Iris adhesions to the anterior lens capsule giving an irregular, festooned pupil are posterior synechiae.
optionExplanations.D: Hypopyon is the gravitational layering of purulent inflammatory white blood cells in the inferior anterior chamber.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify posterior synechiae as inflammatory adhesions between the iris margin and the anterior lens capsule, causing pupil irregularity.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man of Mediterranean descent presents with severe bilateral eye pain, redness, perilimbal injection, and blurred vision. Review of systems reveals a history of recurrent, painful oral aphthous ulcers occurring 4 times a year, painful genital ulcers, and tender erythematous skin nodules on his shins (erythema nodosum). Ophthalmic examination demonstrates nongranulomatous anterior uveitis with a shifting hypopyon, accompanied by retinal occlusive vasculitis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Behçet disease is a systemic, relapsing, multi-organ autoimmune vasculitis most prevalent along the historic 'Silk Road' (Mediterranean, Middle East, East Asia), strongly linked to the HLA-B51 allele. Its diagnostic hallmark is recurrent, painful aphthous oral ulcers combined with at least two of the following: recurrent genital ulcers, ocular inflammation (anterior/posterior/panuveitis, retinal vasculitis), skin lesions (erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis), or a positive pathergy test. Ocular involvement occurs in ~70% of patients and classically manifests as an explosive, nongranulomatous bilateral panuveitis with a 'cold' shifting hypopyon (transient, sterile, non-coagulated pus in the anterior chamber) and occlusive retinal branch vasculitis.

HIGH-YIELD: Behçet Disease Triad & Hallmarks:
• Oral aphthae (universal) + Genital aphthae + Ocular inflammation (Panuveitis with shifting hypopyon & retinal vasculitis).
• Genetic Association: HLA-B51.
• Pathergy test: Pustule formation 24–48 hours after sterile needle skin prick.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Behçet's hypopyon is sterile, highly mobile ('shifting' with head position), and resolves rapidly with systemic immunosuppression; do not confuse it with infectious endophthalmitis!

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Recurrent oral and genital ulcers, erythema nodosum, a shifting hypopyon and retinal occlusive vasculitis in a young man of Mediterranean descent indicate Behcet disease.
optionExplanations.B: Viral keratitis is typically unilateral, features dendritic corneal ulcers, and does not cause recurrent oral/genital ulcers or retinal vasculitis.
optionExplanations.C: Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with an unreactive mid-dilated pupil, shallow anterior chamber, and extremely high IOP (>50 mmHg) without aphthae.
optionExplanations.D: Sympathetic ophthalmia is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis following penetrating trauma or surgery to the contralateral eye.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose panuveitis secondary to Behçet disease by the constellation of recurrent oral/genital ulcers, erythema nodosum, and uveitis with shifting hypopyon.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man presents with acute, painful redness and photophobia in his left eye. He reports a 3-year history of chronic lower back pain and morning stiffness that lasts >1 hour and improves with physical exercise but worsens with rest. Pelvic radiography demonstrates bilateral sacroiliitis. Which genetic marker is strongly linked to this patient's underlying condition?
questions.explanation:
This patient has ankylosing spondylitis (AS), a chronic seronegative spondyloarthropathy strongly associated (>90% of cases) with the major histocompatibility complex class I allele HLA-B27. The clinical presentation of chronic inflammatory back pain (morning stiffness improving with exercise) combined with radiographic sacroiliitis is pathognomonic. Acute anterior uveitis (AAU / iridocyclitis) is the single most common extra-articular manifestation of AS, occurring in 25%–40% of patients. It characteristically presents as unilateral, acute, sudden-onset, recurrent, nongranulomatous anterior uveitis with ciliary injection, intense photophobia, cells/flare in the anterior chamber, and posterior synechiae.

HIGH-YIELD: Seronegative HLA-B27 Spondyloarthropathies ('PAIR'):
• P = Psoriatic Arthritis
• A = Ankylosing Spondylitis (>90% HLA-B27 positive)
• I = Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Crohn's, Ulcerative Colitis)
• R = Reactive Arthritis (formerly Reiter's: Urethritis, Conjunctivitis/Uveitis, Arthritis).
• Ocular presentation: Recurrent, unilateral, alternating acute anterior uveitis.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: HLA-B27 uveitis is typically non-granulomatous, acute, and alternates between eyes across separate attacks; it rarely affects both eyes simultaneously in the same episode.

optionExplanations.A: Option A & B: Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are positive in rheumatoid arthritis (seropositive arthropathy), whereas ankylosing spondylitis is seronegative (RF negative).
optionExplanations.B: Option A & B: Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are positive in rheumatoid arthritis (seropositive arthropathy), whereas ankylosing spondylitis is seronegative (RF negative).
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Inflammatory back pain with sacroiliitis (ankylosing spondylitis) and acute anterior uveitis is associated with HLA-B27.
optionExplanations.D: HLA-DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and giant cell arteritis, not seronegative spondyloarthropathies.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify HLA-B27 as the genetic marker for ankylosing spondylitis presenting with inflammatory back pain and acute anterior uveitis.

questions.question: A 6-year-old girl with a 6-month history of swelling in her right knee and left ankle is diagnosed with oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). Laboratory workup reveals positive ANA (1:640) and negative RF. She is entirely free of any visual complaints, eye redness, or photophobia. What is the most likely associated ophthalmic condition for which urgent screening is indicated?
questions.explanation:
Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA), specifically the oligoarticular subtype in young females with a positive Antinuclear Antibody (ANA), carries a very high risk (up to 20%–30%) of developing chronic, nongranulomatous anterior uveitis. Critically, this uveitis is completely ASYMPTOMATIC ('white and quiet eye'): children do not complain of pain, photophobia, or redness. Because the eye remains uninflamed externally, the insidious chronic intraocular inflammation frequently goes unnoticed until severe, irreversible complications develop: band keratopathy, posterior synechiae, complicated cataract, and secondary glaucoma. Routine slit-lamp screening every 3 months is mandatory for early detection and treatment with topical steroids and methotrexate.

HIGH-YIELD: JIA Uveitis High-Yield Profile:
• Demographics: Young girl (<6 years) + Oligoarticular JIA + Positive ANA + Negative RF.
• Clinical Presentation: COMPLETELY ASYMPTOMATIC ('Silent Uveitis', eye is white and quiet!).
• Complications if unscreened: Band keratopathy + Cataract + Secondary glaucoma.
• Screening Protocol: Mandatory slit-lamp biomicroscopy every 3 months!

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Do NOT wait for red eye or eye complaints to refer a child with JIA to an ophthalmologist; the classic exam trap is that JIA uveitis is completely silent until the child is blind!

optionExplanations.A: Acute painful uveitis with redness and photophobia is typical of HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies, NOT JIA (which is classic for its silent, white-eye presentation).
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Oligoarticular JIA with a positive ANA carries a high risk of chronic, asymptomatic anterior uveitis, so regular slit-lamp screening is needed even without symptoms.
optionExplanations.C: Allergic conjunctivitis causes itching, papillae, and watery discharge, unrelated to ANA-positive JIA.
optionExplanations.D: Orbital cellulitis is an acute febrile bacterial orbital infection.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that oligoarticular JIA in ANA-positive children is strongly associated with chronic, asymptomatic, sight-threatening anterior uveitis.

questions.question: A 29-year-old patient presents with acute-onset dull, aching eye pain, intense photophobia (pain worsened by light exposure), blurred vision, and perilimbal conjunctival hyperemia in the right eye. The cornea is clear, the pupil is constricted and sluggishly reactive, and intraocular pressure is 11 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Acute anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis) is an inflammation of the iris and ciliary body. The classic clinical presentation includes: (1) aching, deep, throbbing eye pain, (2) marked consensual photophobia (shining light into the unaffected eye causes pain in the affected eye due to consensual pupillary constriction triggering ciliary spasm), (3) perilimbal ciliary flush, (4) blurred vision, and (5) a small, poorly reactive pupil (miosis secondary to iris sphincter spasm). Slit-lamp biomicroscopy confirms the diagnosis by visualizing leukocytes (cells) and protein leakage (flare) suspended in the anterior chamber, along with keratic precipitates (KPs) on the corneal endothelium.

HIGH-YIELD: Anterior Uveitis Diagnostic Hallmarks:
• Symptoms: Deep aching pain + Consensual photophobia + Blurred vision.
• Signs: Circumcorneal (ciliary) flush + Miosis + Anterior chamber cells & flare + Keratic precipitates.
• Initial Medical Therapy: Topical Prednisolone acetate 1% (anti-inflammatory) + Cyclopentolate/Atropine (cycloplegia relieves pain and prevents synechiae).

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Consensual photophobia is a pathognomonic clinical pearl for anterior uveitis: Pain in the diseased eye when light is shone into the HEALTHY eye confirms ciliary body inflammation, ruling out superficial conjunctivitis!

optionExplanations.A: Conjunctivitis causes superficial discharge and grittiness without photophobia, ciliary flush, or anterior chamber cells.
optionExplanations.B: Bacterial keratitis exhibits a prominent, white, focal corneal stromal infiltrate staining with fluorescein.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Aching pain, photophobia, perilimbal hyperemia, a clear cornea, a constricted sluggish pupil and low IOP indicate acute anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis).
optionExplanations.D: Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with severe headache, nausea/vomiting, a mid-dilated non-reactive pupil, cloudy edematous cornea, and highly elevated IOP (>50 mmHg; here IOP is low-normal at 11 mmHg due to ciliary body hyposecretion).

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose acute anterior uveitis by the classic constellation of ciliary flush, photophobia, aching eye pain, miosis, and anterior chamber cells.

questions.question: A patient with severe intraocular inflammation presents with a visible horizontal fluid level consisting of white purulent sediment accumulated in the inferior dependent portion of the anterior chamber. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A hypopyon is a visible collection of inflammatory cells (primarily polymorphonuclear leukocytes / neutrophils) layered gravitationally at the bottom of the anterior chamber, forming a characteristic horizontal white-to-yellow fluid level behind the clear lower cornea. It signifies intense, severe anterior chamber inflammation and can be infectious (endophthalmitis, severe bacterial or fungal corneal ulcer) or non-infectious / sterile (HLA-B27 acute anterior uveitis, Behçet disease, systemic inflammatory disease).

HIGH-YIELD: Hypopyon Etiology Classification:
• Infectious: Endophthalmitis (post-surgical, post-injection, traumatic, or endogenous septic emboli), Microbial Keratitis.
• Non-infectious (Sterile): HLA-B27 associated anterior uveitis, Behçet disease (classic shifting hypopyon).

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Never confuse hypopyon (white blood cells/pus, yellow-white fluid line) with hyphema (red blood cells, red fluid line).

optionExplanations.A: Hyphema is a collection of red blood cells (erythrocytes) forming a red fluid level in the anterior chamber, typically following blunt trauma.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A layered white sediment of inflammatory cells at the bottom of the anterior chamber is a hypopyon (blood would be a hyphema).
optionExplanations.C: Keratic precipitates are microscopic cellular clumps adhering to the corneal endothelium, not a layered fluid level.
optionExplanations.D: Posterior synechiae are iris-lens adhesions causing pupil irregularity.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify hypopyon as the gravitational layering of purulent white blood cells in the inferior anterior chamber.

questions.question: A 7-year-old girl is diagnosed with oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). She has a 6-month history of morning stiffness and inflammatory arthritis involving her right knee and left wrist, with a positive ANA titer. All of the following clinical statements regarding this condition are FALSE, EXCEPT:

options.A: The ocular manifestation most commonly associated is posterior chorioretinitis
options.B: The ocular manifestation most commonly associated is demyelinating optic neuritis
options.C: The ocular manifestation most commonly associated is chronic anterior uveitis
options.D: Exudative retinal detachment is a frequent early presenting finding

questions.explanation:
Chronic anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis) is the quintessential and overwhelmingly most common ocular manifestation of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA). It occurs predominantly in young girls with oligoarticular arthritis (<4 joints involved) who are antinuclear antibody (ANA) positive and rheumatoid factor (RF) negative. Posterior segment involvement (chorioretinitis or retinal detachment) and optic neuritis are extremely rare. Because JIA anterior uveitis is indolent and clinically 'quiet' without pain or redness, routine slit-lamp biomicroscopy every 3 months is essential to prevent permanent complications.

HIGH-YIELD: JIA Ocular Screening Protocol (American Academy of Pediatrics):
• High Risk: Oligoarticular JIA + ANA positive + age of onset <6 years -> Slit-lamp exam every 3 MONTHS for at least 4 years.
• Medium Risk: Oligoarticular JIA + ANA negative -> Slit-lamp exam every 6 months.
• Low Risk: Systemic onset JIA -> Slit-lamp exam annually.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Systemic-onset JIA (Still's disease: quotidian fevers, salmon-pink rash, hepatosplenomegaly) rarely causes uveitis; oligoarticular ANA+ JIA is the classic high-risk phenotype!

optionExplanations.A: Posterior uveitis is typical of toxoplasmosis, CMV, or sarcoidosis, not JIA.
optionExplanations.B: Optic neuritis is associated with multiple sclerosis or MOG antibody disease.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (the only true statement): chronic anterior uveitis is the most common ocular manifestation of JIA; the other statements are false.
optionExplanations.D: Retinal detachment is not an early feature of JIA.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize chronic anterior uveitis as the most common ocular manifestation associated with juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

questions.question: A 31-year-old patient presents with acute unilateral anterior uveitis in his right eye (ciliary flush, 3+ anterior chamber cells, miosis, and photophobia). He had an identical episode in the left eye 6 weeks ago that resolved completely. After ruling out infectious keratitis, what is the most appropriate first-line medical management?

options.B: Topical corticosteroid drops (e.g., prednisolone acetate 1%) combined with a cycloplegic agent
options.D: Observation only, as acute uveitis is self-limiting without long-term risk

questions.explanation:
The cornerstone first-line medical therapy for non-infectious acute anterior uveitis consists of: (1) Topical corticosteroids: High-potency, lipophilic topical steroids with excellent corneal penetration (e.g., Prednisolone acetate 1% or Dexamethasone 0.1%) instilled frequently (every 1–2 hours initially) to suppress intraocular inflammation, reduce leukocyte extravasation, and stabilize the blood-aqueous barrier. (2) Topical cycloplegics/mydriatics: Agents such as Cyclopentolate 1% or Atropine 1% are co-administered to immobilize the ciliary muscle (relieving agonizing ciliary spasm and photophobia) and to dilate the pupil, preventing and breaking sight-threatening posterior synechiae.

HIGH-YIELD: Anterior Uveitis Dual Pharmacotherapy: 1. Topical Steroid (Prednisolone acetate 1%) -> Anti-inflammatory; taper slowly as anterior chamber cells clear. 2. Topical Cycloplegic (Cyclopentolate 1% TID or Atropine 1% BID) -> Paralyzes ciliary muscle (pain relief) + Dilates pupil (prevents posterior synechiae).

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Always taper topical steroids gradually in anterior uveitis; abrupt discontinuation triggers acute rebound intraocular inflammation!

optionExplanations.A: Acyclovir is indicated only for confirmed herpetic uveitis (typically associated with high IOP, corneal dendrites, and iris atrophy).
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Non-infectious acute anterior uveitis is treated with topical corticosteroids to control inflammation plus a cycloplegic agent for pain and to prevent posterior synechiae.
optionExplanations.C: Antibiotics are completely ineffective for non-infectious autoimmune anterior uveitis.
optionExplanations.D: Observation is unacceptable; untreated anterior uveitis leads to permanent posterior synechiae, inflammatory glaucoma, cataracts, and cystoid macular edema.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify topical corticosteroids combined with a cycloplegic agent as the first-line treatment for acute anterior uveitis.

questions.question: A 28-year-old obese woman presents with chronic throbbing headaches that are worse in the morning, pulsatile tinnitus (whooshing sounds in her ears), transient visual obscurations (brief episodes of vision dimming when bending over), and horizontal diplopia. Fundoscopy demonstrates bilateral, symmetric optic disc swelling with blurred disc margins, flame hemorrhages, and absence of spontaneous venous pulsations. Brain MRI is normal and lumbar puncture shows opening pressure of 340 mm H2O with normal CSF composition. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Papilledema secondary to elevated intracranial pressure (Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension)
options.B: Bilateral non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy

questions.explanation:
Papilledema is strictly defined as bilateral optic disc swelling secondary to elevated intracranial pressure (ICP). In idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH / pseudotumor cerebri), elevated ICP is transmitted directly along the perioptic subarachnoid space, compressing the unmyelinated optic nerve axons at the lamina cribrosa and interrupting axoplasmic transport. The clinical hallmarks are: (1) bilateral symmetric disc edema with obscuration of retinal vessels, (2) transient visual obscurations lasting seconds, (3) pulsatile tinnitus, (4) CN VI palsy (false localizing sign due to stretching along the petroclival ligament), and (5) normal visual acuity in early stages with enlarged physiological blind spots on visual field testing.

HIGH-YIELD: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH) Profile:
• Patient: 'Female, Fat, Fertile, Forty'. Associated with Tetracyclines, excess Vitamin A/Retinoids, Growth hormone.
• Diagnosis: Modified Dandy Criteria (Symptoms of high ICP, normal neuroimaging, elevated opening pressure >250 mm H2O, normal CSF composition).
• First-line Medical Therapy: Weight loss + Oral Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor reduces CSF production).

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Visual acuity is CHARACTERISTICALLY NORMAL in early and moderate papilledema! Do not assume normal 20/20 vision rules out severe intracranial hypertension.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Bilateral disc swelling with headache, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations, diplopia and an opening pressure of 340 mm H2O with normal CSF indicates papilledema from idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
optionExplanations.B: NAION is typically unilateral in older vasculopathic patients (>50 years) presenting with sudden, painless, irreversible altitudinal visual field loss.
optionExplanations.C: Optic neuritis is usually unilateral, painful with eye movement, and causes severe early drop in visual acuity and central scotoma.
optionExplanations.D: CRVO presents with unilateral massive retinal flame hemorrhages ('blood and thunder').

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize bilateral optic disc edema in a patient with elevated intracranial pressure as papilledema, characteristically presenting with preserved visual acuity and transient visual obscurations.

questions.question: A 56-year-old diabetic patient is treated for diffuse diabetic macular edema (DME). Fundus examination reveals a pattern of light, small, evenly spaced laser burns placed across the edematous macula while strictly avoiding the foveal avascular zone. Which specific type of laser photocoagulation is utilized for this treatment?
questions.explanation:
Grid macular photocoagulation involves applying a grid pattern of light-intensity, small spot-size (50–100 µm) laser burns throughout areas of diffuse retinal thickening and capillary non-perfusion in the macula, while carefully preserving the central 500 µm foveal avascular zone (FAZ). Historically validated by the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) for clinically significant macular edema (CSME), grid laser stimulates retinal pigment epithelial pump function and reduces vascular permeability (today largely complemented or superseded by first-line anti-VEGF intravitreal therapy).

HIGH-YIELD: Retinal Laser Types:
• Focal / Grid Laser: Applied to MACULA for macular edema / microaneurysm closure (spares fovea).
• Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP): Applied to PERIPHERY for proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) or ischemic CRVO.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Never apply laser to the foveal avascular zone (FAZ); doing so produces an immediate, permanent, irreversible central scotoma!

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Diffuse diabetic macular edema is treated with grid macular photocoagulation: light, evenly spaced burns that spare the foveal avascular zone.
optionExplanations.B: Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) applies 1,200–1,800 large burns (200–500 µm) across the peripheral and mid-peripheral retina to treat neovascularization in proliferative retinopathy, strictly sparing the entire macula.
optionExplanations.C: Nd:YAG laser iridotomy creates a hole in the peripheral iris for angle-closure glaucoma.
optionExplanations.D: Excimer laser ablates corneal stroma to correct refractive errors.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify grid laser photocoagulation as a treatment applied across the macula to treat diffuse diabetic macular edema.

questions.question: A 24-year-old patient presents with floaters and blurred vision in the right eye. Dilated fundus examination reveals a creamy-yellow, fluffy, focal necrotizing retinochoroidal lesion immediately adjacent to an old, heavily pigmented, atrophic chorioretinal scar ('satellite lesion'). Vitreous haze is prominent directly overlying the lesion, producing the classic 'headlight in the fog' appearance. What is the most common causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Toxoplasma gondii (an obligate intracellular protozoan parasite) is the most common cause of infectious posterior uveitis in immunocompetent individuals worldwide. Humans acquire infection by ingesting undercooked meat containing tissue cysts or through accidental ingestion of oocysts shed in feline feces. The classic, pathognomonic fundus finding is an active focal white-yellow necrotizing retinochoroiditis developing immediately adjacent to an old, hyperpigmented chorioretinal scar (a 'satellite lesion'). Dense overlying vitreous inflammatory debris gives rise to the classic 'headlight in the fog' appearance.

HIGH-YIELD: Ocular Toxoplasmosis Hallmarks:
• Classic Sign: 'Headlight in the fog' (Active retinitis viewed through dense vitreous haze) + Satellite lesion next to old pigmented scar.
• Classic Triple Drug Therapy: Pyrimethamine + Sulfadiazine + Folinic acid (Leucovorin, to prevent bone marrow suppression) + Oral Corticosteroids (added after initiating antiparasitics). Alternative: Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim) + Clindamycin.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Never administer systemic corticosteroids as monotherapy in toxoplasmosis; steroids without antiparasitic coverage cause explosive parasitic replication and devastating retinal destruction!

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A focal necrotizing retinochoroiditis adjacent to an old pigmented scar ('headlight in the fog') is classic for Toxoplasma gondii.
optionExplanations.B: Herpes simplex virus causes acute retinal necrosis (ARN) with rapidly progressive, confluent peripheral necrotizing retinitis and occlusive vasculitis.
optionExplanations.C: Treponema pallidum is the 'great imitator,' presenting with placoid chorioretinitis or panuveitis, but not focal satellite recurrence next to a pigmented scar.
optionExplanations.D: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis occurs in severely immunocompromised patients (CD4 <50) with 'pizza-pie' / 'cottage cheese and ketchup' perivascular hemorrhagic necrosis.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize Toxoplasma gondii as the most common cause of posterior uveitis, characterized by an active necrotizing satellite lesion adjacent to an old chorioretinal scar.

questions.question: An 18-month-old child is brought in by his parents, who noticed an abnormal white pupil reflection in flash photography. On examination, there is right-sided esotropia, absence of the normal red reflex (leukocoria), and a solid, pinkish-white, nodular retinal mass protruding into the vitreous cavity with prominent intrinsic calcification on B-scan ultrasound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, originating from primitive neuroectodermal retinal cells. It typically presents before 2 years of age (median age of diagnosis: 12 months for bilateral/ hereditary, 24 months for unilateral/sporadic). The two most common presenting clinical signs are: (1) Leukocoria ('white pupil' / cat's eye reflex, seen in ~60%), and (2) Strabismus (in ~20%, caused by tumor involvement of the fovea disrupting central fixation). The pathognomonic feature on B-scan ultrasonography or orbital CT is intrinsic intra-tumoral calcification (calcified mass in a child <3 years old is virtually diagnostic of retinoblastoma).

HIGH-YIELD: Retinoblastoma Genetics & Presentation:
• Genetics: Bi-allelic mutation/inactivation of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 13q14 (Knudson two-hit hypothesis).
• Two most common signs: 1st = Leukocoria (60%); 2nd = Strabismus (20%).
• Imaging of choice: MRI of brain and orbits (detects trilateral retinoblastoma [pinealoblastoma] and avoids CT radiation which induces secondary osteosarcomas!).

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: NEVER perform a fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) or intraocular paracentesis in suspected retinoblastoma: Violating the ocular coats causes catastrophic extraocular tumor seeding!

optionExplanations.A: Congenital cataracts cause leukocoria but are located within the crystalline lens and show zero intraocular retinal mass or calcifications.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Leukocoria with strabismus and a calcified intraocular retinal mass on B-scan in a young child is retinoblastoma.
optionExplanations.C: Persistent fetal vasculature features a microphthalmic eye with a fibrovascular retrolental stalk pulling ciliary processes centrally.
optionExplanations.D: Coats disease presents in slightly older boys (6–8 years) with unilateral retinal telangiectasias and massive subretinal exudation, typically without large calcified tumor masses.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose retinoblastoma in a toddler presenting with leukocoria, strabismus, and an intraocular calcified retinal mass.

questions.question: A 58-year-old patient with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents with profound visual loss. Fundus examination demonstrates extensive retinal ischemia, neovascularization of the disc (NVD), and a layered preretinal and vitreous hemorrhage obscuring the macula. What is the standard evidence-based management strategy?

options.A: Combination therapy with Intravitreal Anti-VEGF injections and Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP)

questions.explanation:
Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) with high-risk characteristics (NVD ≥1/4 to 1/3 disc area, or any NVD/NVE with vitreous/preretinal hemorrhage) demands urgent intervention. Chronic microvascular retinal non-perfusion drives massive intraocular overexpression of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF). Combining intravitreal anti-VEGF agents (e.g., Aflibercept, Ranibizumab, Bevacizumab) with Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) is the premier standard of care: anti-VEGF injections induce rapid regression and closure of fragile neovascular fronds within days, clearing hemorrhages, while PRP permanently ablates the ischemic, oxygen-consuming peripheral retina to permanently reduce baseline VEGF production.

HIGH-YIELD: PDR High-Risk Characteristics (DRS Criteria): 1. NVD ≥1/4 to 1/3 disc area. 2. Any NVD with associated vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage. 3. NVE ≥1/2 disc area with vitreous/preretinal hemorrhage.
• Presence of any high-risk criterion mandates immediate treatment to prevent severe vision loss!

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: If extensive vitreoretinal fibrovascular traction bands are present, administering anti-VEGF alone can cause rapid fibrosis and contracture of the neovascular membrane ('crunch syndrome'), tearing the retina and causing tractional detachment!

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy with disc neovascularization and vitreous hemorrhage is managed with panretinal photocoagulation, combined with intravitreal anti-VEGF per the source.
optionExplanations.B: Anti-VEGF alone requires continuous, strict monthly injections indefinitely; if patients miss follow-up visits, rapid rebound neovascularization and tractional retinal detachment can occur.
optionExplanations.C: PRP alone can be difficult to deliver through dense vitreous hemorrhage and can acutely worsen macular edema; pre-treatment with anti-VEGF facilitates PRP delivery.
optionExplanations.D: Topical medications have zero efficacy in proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize combination therapy with intravitreal anti-VEGF and panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) as the primary treatment for high-risk proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset distortion of straight lines (metamorphopsia) and a dark gray spot in the center of her visual field (central scotoma) in the right eye over 2 weeks. On Amsler grid testing, straight grid lines appear wavy and bent. Dilated fundus examination and OCT reveal a subretinal choroidal neovascular membrane (CNVM) with subretinal fluid, intraretinal lipid exudates, and hemorrhage. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of permanent, irreversible legal blindness among individuals aged >60 years in developed countries. Wet (neovascular / exudative) AMD accounts for only ~10%–15% of all AMD cases but is responsible for >80%–90% of severe, acute visual loss. It is driven by the pathological growth of abnormal, fragile new blood vessels from the choroid through breaks in Bruch's membrane into the sub-RPE or subretinal space (Choroidal Neovascularization, CNVM). These incompetent vessels leak fluid and blood, causing acute metamorphopsia (straight lines appearing wavy on Amsler grid), rapid central vision loss, and subretinal scarring (disciform scar) if untreated. First-line therapy is prompt intravitreal anti-VEGF injections.

HIGH-YIELD: Dry vs. Wet AMD Summary:
• Dry AMD (85–90%): Drusen (yellow extracellular deposits between RPE and Bruch's) + Geographic atrophy. Slow central decline. Treatment: AREDS-2 formula vitamins (vitamins C & E, zinc, copper, lutein, zeaxanthin).
• Wet AMD (10–15%): CNVM break through Bruch's membrane -> Subretinal hemorrhage & fluid -> Rapid vision loss & metamorphopsia. Treatment: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF injections (Aflibercept, Ranibizumab, Faricimab).

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Metamorphopsia (grid lines curving) is the earliest and most sensitive symptom of wet AMD; all dry AMD patients should self-monitor with an Amsler grid at home!

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Metamorphopsia, central scotoma and a subretinal choroidal neovascular membrane with fluid, exudate and hemorrhage indicate wet (neovascular) AMD.
optionExplanations.B: Dry AMD is chronic and slowly progressive (over years), characterized by soft drusen and geographic atrophy of the RPE/choriocapillaris without neovascular leakage or hemorrhage.
optionExplanations.C: Central serous chorioretinopathy occurs in young-to-middle-aged men (20–50 years) with high stress/steroid use, presenting with idiopathic serous neurosensory detachment without CNVM.
optionExplanations.D: Glaucoma causes painless peripheral visual field loss, completely sparing central vision until the end stage.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose wet (neovascular) AMD in an elderly patient presenting with acute metamorphopsia, central scotoma, and choroidal neovascularization.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with a history of carotid atherosclerosis and atrial fibrillation presents with sudden, catastrophic, painless, complete loss of vision in his left eye of 6 hours duration. Visual acuity is count fingers at 1 foot, and a prominent left relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is present. Dilated fundus examination reveals marked diffuse whitening and opacification of the posterior pole retina with a distinct, sharply demarcated 'cherry-red spot' at the fovea. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) is an acute ophthalmologic emergency analogous to an acute ischemic stroke of the eye. It is most commonly caused by thromboembolism originating from ipsilateral carotid artery atheromas (cholesterol Hollenhorst plaques), cardiac valves, or aortic arch. Occlusion halts blood flow through the central retinal artery, causing acute ischemia and intracellular cytotoxic edema of the inner two-thirds of the retina (nerve fiber, ganglion cell, and inner plexiform layers), which turns the retina opaque, pale, and milky-white. The fovea, however, is extremely thin, lacking inner retinal layers; the underlying rich vascular choroid (supplied by posterior ciliary arteries) shines brightly through the thin foveal depression, creating the classic pathognomonic 'cherry-red spot'.

HIGH-YIELD: CRAO Management Essentials:
• Presentation: Sudden, painless, profound monocular vision loss + RAPD + Pale retina with 'Cherry-Red Spot'.
• Emergency window: Irreversible retinal damage occurs after 90–240 minutes of complete ischemia.
• Acute maneuvers: Ocular massage, anterior chamber paracentesis, sublingual isosorbide, hyperbaric oxygen (all have limited proven efficacy).
• MANDATORY WORKUP: Emergent stroke workup (Carotid Doppler, Echocardiogram, Holter monitor) + ESR/CRP to rule out Giant Cell Arteritis in patients >50 years!

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: If a cilioretinal artery is present (present in ~15–20% of the population, derived from the posterior ciliary circulation), a small island of central macular vision (20/20) will be dramatically spared despite total peripheral blindness!

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Sudden painless monocular vision loss with a RAPD, diffuse retinal whitening and a cherry-red spot is central retinal artery occlusion.
optionExplanations.B: CRVO presents with extensive retinal hemorrhages in all four quadrants ('blood and thunder') and engorged tortuous veins, not retinal whitening.
optionExplanations.C: BRAO produces a localized, segmental, wedge-shaped zone of retinal whitening confined to a single arteriolar branch.
optionExplanations.D: Retinal detachment shows an undulating, wrinkled, mobile neurosensory retinal flap, not a cherry-red spot.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) by acute, profound, painless vision loss accompanied by diffuse retinal whitening and a foveal cherry-red spot.

questions.question: A 52-year-old patient with severe, end-stage proliferative diabetic retinopathy presents complaining of progressive floaters and a persistent visual field shadowing that has expanded over several weeks. Dilated fundus examination reveals dense, thick, taut, contracted fibrovascular vitreous membranes pulling and tenting the underlying retina forward into a concave, immobile, localized elevation. No retinal tears or holes are identified. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Retinal detachments are classified into three distinct pathophysiological types: (1) Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD): caused by mechanical contraction of fibrovascular proliferative membranes adhering to the retina (most commonly seen in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, retinopathy of prematurity, or sickle cell retinopathy). The retina appears concave, smooth, taut, and elevated along vascular arcades; it lacks retinal breaks, does not shift with gravity, and does not extend to the ora serrata. Definitive treatment requires pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling. (2) Rhegmatogenous (RRD): full-thickness tear allows liquefied vitreous into subretinal space. (3) Exudative: fluid accumulation without tears or traction (uveitis, tumors).

HIGH-YIELD: Retinal Detachment Classification:
• Rhegmatogenous (RRD): Break/Tear present -> Vitreous fluid enters -> Convex, undulating, mobile (most common!).
• Tractional (TRD): Fibrovascular membrane contracts -> Mechanically pulls retina -> Concave, taut, immobile, NO TEAR (Diabetes!).
• Exudative (ERD): Subretinal fluid leakage from vessels/tumors -> Shifting fluid, smooth, NO TEAR, NO TRACTION.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: If a tractional detachment develops a secondary retinal tear (tractional rhegmatogenous detachment), it becomes an acute surgical emergency because fluid rapidly detaches the entire retina.

optionExplanations.A: Rhegmatogenous detachment requires a full-thickness break (hole/tear), has a convex and corrugated/undulating surface, and is mobile.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Taut fibrovascular membranes pulling the retina into a concave, immobile elevation with no retinal breaks indicate traction retinal detachment.
optionExplanations.C: Exudative detachment is characterized by smooth, shifting subretinal fluid that moves instantly with gravity and patient repositioning.
optionExplanations.D: Central serous chorioretinopathy is a localized, small serous macular detachment in young adults.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate traction retinal detachment (concave, taut elevation without retinal tears caused by contracting fibrovascular membranes) from rhegmatogenous detachment.

questions.question: A wide-field fundus photograph of a diabetic patient demonstrates hundreds of scattered, circular, chorioretinal laser scars distributed across all four peripheral and mid-peripheral quadrants, while the central posterior pole and macula remain entirely untouched. What procedure has been performed?
questions.explanation:
Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) is the cornerstone ablative laser therapy for proliferative retinopathies, most notably proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) and ischemic central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). By applying 1,200 to 1,800 thermal laser burns across the ischemic peripheral retina, PRP intentionally destroys high-oxygen-consuming photoreceptors and ischemic retinal tissue, replacing them with avascular glial scars. This significantly decreases the total metabolic demand of the eye, eliminates the primary stimulus for VEGF production, and promotes dramatic, permanent involution and regression of fragile neovascular vessels.

HIGH-YIELD: PRP Mechanism & Side Effects:
• Mechanism: Destroys ischemic peripheral retina -> Decreases ocular VEGF production -> Induces regression of neovascularization (NVD/NVE).
• Known Side Effects: Mild reduction in peripheral visual field, loss of dark adaptation (night blindness), and temporary exacerbation of macular edema.

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: PRP strictly spares the central macula within the major temporal vascular arcades to preserve reading vision and visual acuity.

optionExplanations.A: Nd:YAG laser posterior capsulotomy creates an opening in the posterior lens capsule for post-cataract opacification.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Hundreds of scattered peripheral and mid-peripheral laser scars sparing the macula are the result of panretinal photocoagulation (PRP).
optionExplanations.C: SLT applies laser burns to the trabecular meshwork to lower IOP in open-angle glaucoma.
optionExplanations.D: Focal macular laser applies small burns specifically in the macula for diabetic macular edema.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) as the pattern of scattered peripheral chorioretinal laser burns used to treat retinal neovascularization.

questions.question: A 66-year-old woman presents with sudden central visual distortion and a round, blind spot when looking directly at faces with her right eye. Fundoscopy reveals a sharply circumscribed, round, reddish defect directly in the center of the fovea, surrounded by a gray halo of subretinal fluid and fine yellow drusen-like deposits at the base. Shining a thin slit-beam across the fovea causes the patient to report a distinct break or notch in the vertical beam (positive Watzke-Allen sign). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
