questions.question: A 27-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively decreasing vision in her right eye. She reports a dull, aching pain located behind the eye that is exacerbated by eye movements. On examination, visual acuity is 20/100, and she notes that red stop signs appear 'washed out and brownish-gray' when viewed with the right eye. A right relative afferent pupillary defect is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Optic neuritis is an acute inflammatory, demyelinating disorder of the optic nerve, strongly linked to multiple sclerosis (MS; it is the presenting symptom in 20% of MS patients and occurs in 50% during their lifetime). The classic diagnostic triad consists of: (1) subacute, progressive, unilateral central vision loss peaking over several days to 2 weeks, (2) periocular pain exacerbated by eye movements (caused by traction of the superior and medial recti origins on the richly innervated dura of the optic nerve sheath at the annulus of Zinn), and (3) profound dyschromatopsia out of proportion to visual acuity loss (red desaturation). Brain MRI with gadolinium demonstrates optic nerve enhancement and evaluates for periventricular white matter demyelinating plaques.

HIGH-YIELD: Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) Guidelines:
• Treatment: IV Methylprednisolone (1,000 mg/day for 3 days) followed by oral prednisone taper accelerates visual recovery.
• CONTRAINDICATION: Oral Prednisone ALONE is STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED because it doubles the rate of recurrent optic neuritis attacks!

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: Never prescribe low-dose oral prednisone monotherapy for optic neuritis; you must use high-dose IV corticosteroids followed by oral taper.

optionExplanations.A: NAION occurs in older patients (>50 years) with vascular risk factors; it presents with sudden, painless altitudinal visual loss without pain on eye movement.
optionExplanations.B: Toxic neuropathy (e.g., ethambutol, methanol) is bilateral, painless, progressive, and lacks pain on eye movement.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Subacute vision loss with pain on eye movement, red desaturation and a RAPD in a young woman indicates optic neuritis, commonly associated with multiple sclerosis.
optionExplanations.D: IIH causes bilateral papilledema, headaches, and pulsatile tinnitus with preserved visual acuity.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize optic neuritis in a young woman presenting with subacute monocular vision loss, pain on eye movement, and red desaturation.

questions.question: In thyroid eye disease (Graves' orbitopathy), autoimmune infiltration and glycosaminoglycan expansion cause restrictive myopathy of the extraocular muscles. Which extraocular muscle is commonly the SECOND most severely and frequently affected?
questions.explanation:
Extraocular muscle enlargement and restrictive fibrosis in thyroid eye disease follow a well-characterized, highly reproducible hierarchical pattern remembered by the classic clinical mnemonic 'I'M SLOw': (1) Inferior rectus (most common, ~60%–70%; restricts upgaze, causing hypotropia), (2) Medial rectus (second most common, ~50%–60%; restricts abduction, causing esotropia), (3) Superior rectus (third most common; restricts downgaze), (4) Lateral rectus (least common of the recti), and (5) Oblique muscles (rarely affected). Therefore, the medial rectus is the second most commonly affected muscle.

HIGH-YIELD: Thyroid Eye Disease Muscle Involvement ('I'M SLOw'):
• I = Inferior Rectus (1st, most common -> upgaze limitation)
• M = Medial Rectus (2nd most common -> abduction limitation / esotropia)
• S = Superior Rectus (3rd)
• L = Lateral Rectus (4th)
• O = Obliques (rarely involved).

EXAM TRAP / DO NOT MISS: CT or MRI finding: Characteristically shows enlargement of the muscle BELLIES with SPARING of the muscle tendons ('coca-cola bottle sign'); involvement of both belly and tendon indicates orbital pseudotumor (myositis)!

optionExplanations.A: The inferior rectus is the FIRST (most common) muscle affected.
optionExplanations.B: The superior rectus is the third most commonly affected muscle.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. In thyroid eye disease the usual order of muscle involvement is inferior rectus, then medial rectus, then superior rectus ('I'M SLOw').
optionExplanations.D: The lateral rectus is the least commonly affected rectus muscle.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall the hierarchy of extraocular muscle involvement in thyroid eye disease ('I'M SLOw') to identify the medial rectus as the second most commonly affected muscle.
